stem: Mention the advantages of selecting pea plant for experiment by Mendel.
solution:
The garden pea suited Mendel's hybridisation experiments for the following reasons:

1. **Distinct contrasting traits:** many characters occur as two opposing traits, e.g., tall or dwarf plants, yellow or green seeds, round or wrinkled seeds. Mendel studied **seven pairs** of such traits (stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape, seed colour).
2. **True-breeding lines:** continuous **self-pollination** gives true-breeding lines that show stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations; Mendel selected 14 true-breeding varieties.
3. **Easy artificial cross-pollination:** the flower carries both stamens and carpel, so anthers can be removed (**emasculation**) and pollen of the chosen parent transferred to the stigma.
4. **Large number of progeny:** each cross yields many seeds, giving a **large sampling size** and so greater credibility to the data.
5. **Short life cycle** and **easy cultivation**, so successive generations (\(\text{F}_1\), \(\text{F}_2\) and beyond) can be raised and studied quickly.
groundedIn: §4.1; Table 4.1; Fig. 4.2 — two opposing traits; true-breeding lines from continuous self-pollination; 14 true-breeding varieties; seven pairs of traits; emasculation and pollen transfer; large sampling size; BEYOND CHAPTER: pea has a short life cycle and is easy to cultivate

stem: Dominance and Recessive
solution:
In a dissimilar pair of factors, the one that expresses itself is **dominant** and the one that is masked is **recessive**.

| Basis of difference | Dominant | Recessive |
|---|---|---|
| Expression in the heterozygote (Tt) | Expressed | Not expressed (masked) |
| Appearance in a cross of true-breeding parents | Seen in the \(\text{F}_1\) | Not seen in the \(\text{F}_1\); reappears in the \(\text{F}_2\) |
| Proportion in a monohybrid \(\text{F}_2\) | 3/4 of the plants | 1/4 of the plants |
| Genotypes that show it | Homozygous (TT) and heterozygous (Tt) | Only homozygous (tt) |
| Nature of the allele | Usually the unmodified, functioning allele (e.g., makes the normal enzyme) | Usually the modified allele (non-functional enzyme or no enzyme) |
| Symbol | Capital letter, e.g., T (tall) | Small letter, e.g., t (dwarf) |
groundedIn: §4.2; §4.2.1; §4.2.2.1 — in a pair of dissimilar factors one dominates; T dominant over t; 3/4 tall and 1/4 dwarf in F2; recessive expressed only when homozygous (stated in the chapter Summary); unmodified functioning allele is dominant, modified allele generally recessive

stem: Homozygous and Heterozygous
solution:
A **homozygous** individual carries two identical alleles of a gene; a **heterozygous** individual carries two dissimilar alleles.

| Basis of difference | Homozygous | Heterozygous |
|---|---|---|
| Allelic pair | Identical alleles, e.g., TT or tt | Dissimilar alleles, e.g., Tt |
| Gametes formed | Only one kind; all gametes are similar | Two kinds, each carrying one allele, in equal proportion |
| Breeding behaviour | True-breeding: on self-pollination the trait is stable over generations | Not true-breeding: on self-pollination the traits segregate (3 tall : 1 dwarf in the \(\text{F}_2\)) |
| Expression | Expresses the trait of its allele (dominant or recessive) | Expresses only the dominant trait (in complete dominance) |
| Example | True-breeding tall (TT) or dwarf (tt) pea | \(\text{F}_1\) hybrid tall pea (Tt) |
groundedIn: §4.1; §4.2; §4.2.2 — true-breeding line; allelic pair identical or homozygous TT and tt; heterozygote Tt; homozygous parent produces all similar gametes while a heterozygous one produces two kinds in equal proportion

stem: Monohybrid and Dihybrid.
solution:
A **monohybrid** is heterozygous for genes controlling **one** character; a **dihybrid** is heterozygous for genes controlling **two** characters.

| Basis of difference | Monohybrid | Dihybrid |
|---|---|---|
| Characters studied | One pair of contrasting traits, e.g., tall/dwarf | Two pairs, e.g., seed colour and seed shape |
| Example cross | TT (tall) \(\times\) tt (dwarf) | RRYY (round, yellow) \(\times\) rryy (wrinkled, green) |
| \(\text{F}_1\) genotype | Tt | RrYy |
| Kinds of gametes of the \(\text{F}_1\) | Two: T and t | Four: RY, Ry, rY and ry |
| \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypic ratio | **3:1** | **9:3:3:1** |
| \(\text{F}_2\) genotypic ratio | 1:2:1 (3 genotypes) | 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 (9 genotypes) |
| Law it led to | Law of Dominance and Law of Segregation | Law of Independent Assortment |
groundedIn: §4.2; §4.2.1; §4.3; §4.3.1; Fig. 4.7 — Tt is a monohybrid and TT x tt a monohybrid cross with 3:1 and 1:2:1; RRYY x rryy gives RrYy; four gamete types RY, Ry, rY, ry; 9:3:3:1; law of independent assortment

stem: A diploid organism is heterozygous for 4 loci, how many types of gametes can be produced?
solution:
**16 types of gametes.**

1. A heterozygous locus produces two kinds of gametes, each carrying one allele (law of segregation).
2. When the loci assort independently, the alleles of each locus combine with those of every other locus in all combinations, as RrYy gives four types (RY, Ry, rY, ry).
3. So the number of gamete types is \(2^n\), where n is the number of heterozygous loci.
4. For 4 loci (e.g., AaBbCcDd): \(2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16\).

This assumes the four loci are not linked.
groundedIn: §4.2.2; §4.3.1 — a heterozygous parent produces two kinds of gametes; independent segregation in RrYy gives four types of gametes RY, Ry, rY and ry

stem: Explain the Law of Dominance using a monohybrid cross.
solution:
**Law of Dominance:** (i) characters are controlled by discrete units called **factors**; (ii) factors occur in **pairs**; (iii) in a dissimilar pair of factors, one member **dominates** (dominant) the other (recessive).

**Monohybrid cross (tall \(\times\) dwarf pea):**

1. Parents: true-breeding tall (TT) \(\times\) true-breeding dwarf (tt).
2. Gametes: T and t.
3. \(\text{F}_1\): all **Tt**, all **tall**. Although the dwarf allele t is present, only T is expressed, so T is dominant over t.
4. \(\text{F}_1\) self-pollinated (Tt \(\times\) Tt); each parent forms T and t gametes in equal proportion:

| Eggs / Pollen | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | TT (tall) | Tt (tall) |
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (dwarf) |

5. \(\text{F}_2\) genotypic ratio TT : Tt : tt = **1:2:1**; phenotypic ratio tall : dwarf = **3:1**.

The law explains why only one parental character appears in the \(\text{F}_1\), why both appear in the \(\text{F}_2\), and the 3:1 proportion at the \(\text{F}_2\).
groundedIn: §4.2; §4.2.1; Fig. 4.3; Fig. 4.4 — law of dominance (i)-(iii); TT x tt gives all tall Tt F1; F2 1/4 TT, 1/2 Tt, 1/4 tt; 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic ratio; law explains F1, F2 and the 3:1 proportion

stem: Define and design a test-cross.
solution:
**Test cross:** a cross in which an organism showing the **dominant phenotype** (whose genotype is to be determined) is crossed with the **recessive parent** (homozygous recessive) instead of being self-crossed. The progeny reveal the genotype of the test organism.

**Design:** a tall pea plant (genotype TT or Tt unknown) is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt).

**Case 1: tall plant is TT**

| Gametes | T | T |
|---|---|---|
| **t** | Tt (tall) | Tt (tall) |
| **t** | Tt (tall) | Tt (tall) |

All offspring are tall: the tall plant is **homozygous dominant (TT)**.

**Case 2: tall plant is Tt**

| Gametes | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (dwarf) |
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (dwarf) |

Half the offspring are tall and half dwarf, **1:1**: the tall plant is **heterozygous (Tt)**.
groundedIn: §4.2; Fig. 4.5 — test cross: an organism showing a dominant phenotype is crossed with the recessive parent instead of self-crossing; Mendel crossed tall F2 plants with dwarf; all dominant progeny means homozygous, half and half means heterozygous

stem: Using a Punnett Square, workout the distribution of phenotypic features in the first filial generation after a cross between a homozygous female and a heterozygous male for a single locus.
solution:
The homozygous female may be homozygous dominant or homozygous recessive, so there are two possible results. Take height in pea: T (tall) dominant over t (dwarf). The heterozygous male (Tt) forms T and t pollen in equal proportion; the homozygous female forms only one kind of egg.

**Case 1: homozygous dominant female (TT) \(\times\) heterozygous male (Tt)**

| Eggs / Pollen | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | TT (tall) | Tt (tall) |
| **T** | TT (tall) | Tt (tall) |

\(\text{F}_1\): genotypes TT : Tt = 1:1; phenotype **all tall** (100% dominant phenotype).

**Case 2: homozygous recessive female (tt) \(\times\) heterozygous male (Tt)**

| Eggs / Pollen | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (dwarf) |
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (dwarf) |

\(\text{F}_1\): genotypes Tt : tt = 1:1; phenotypes **tall : dwarf = 1:1**.
groundedIn: §4.2; §4.2.2; Fig. 4.4 — Punnett square places gametes on two sides; homozygous parent produces all similar gametes, heterozygous one two kinds in equal proportion; T dominant over t

context: When a cross in made between tall plant with yellow seeds (TtYy) and tall plant with green seed (Ttyy), what proportions of phenotype in the offspring could be expected to be
stem: tall and green.
solution:
**3/8 of the offspring are tall and green.**

T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf); Y (yellow) is dominant over y (green).

1. Gametes of TtYy: TY, Ty, tY, ty (1/4 each). Gametes of Ttyy: Ty, ty (1/2 each).
2. Punnett square:

| TtYy gametes / Ttyy gametes | Ty | ty |
|---|---|---|
| **TY** | TTYy (tall, yellow) | TtYy (tall, yellow) |
| **Ty** | TTyy (tall, green) | Ttyy (tall, green) |
| **tY** | TtYy (tall, yellow) | ttYy (dwarf, yellow) |
| **ty** | Ttyy (tall, green) | ttyy (dwarf, green) |

3. Of the 8 equally likely combinations: tall yellow 3, **tall green 3**, dwarf yellow 1, dwarf green 1, i.e., 3:3:1:1.
4. Check by taking each character separately: Tt \(\times\) Tt gives 3/4 tall; Yy \(\times\) yy gives 1/2 green. Tall and green = 3/4 \(\times\) 1/2 = **3/8**.
groundedIn: §4.3; §4.3.1 — Y for dominant yellow and y for recessive green; segregation of one pair is independent of the other; gamete types written on two sides of a Punnett square

context: When a cross in made between tall plant with yellow seeds (TtYy) and tall plant with green seed (Ttyy), what proportions of phenotype in the offspring could be expected to be
stem: dwarf and green.
solution:
**1/8 of the offspring are dwarf and green.**

1. Height: Tt \(\times\) Tt gives TT : Tt : tt = 1:2:1, so dwarf (tt) = **1/4**.
2. Seed colour: Yy \(\times\) yy gives Yy : yy = 1:1, so green (yy) = **1/2**.
3. As the two genes assort independently, dwarf and green (ttyy) = 1/4 \(\times\) 1/2 = **1/8**.

In the Punnett square (gametes TY, Ty, tY, ty of TtYy against Ty, ty of Ttyy), only 1 of the 8 boxes, ty \(\times\) ty, gives ttyy. The full distribution is tall yellow 3/8 : tall green 3/8 : dwarf yellow 1/8 : dwarf green 1/8.
groundedIn: §4.2; §4.3; §4.3.1 — monohybrid F2 1/4 tt; segregation of one pair independent of the other; Y yellow dominant over y green

stem: Two heterozygous parents are crossed. If the two loci are linked what would be the distribution of phenotypic features in \(\text{F}_1\) generation for a dibybrid cross?
solution:
When the two loci are **linked** they do not assort independently, so the progeny do **not** show the 9:3:3:1 ratio. The **parental combinations** appear in much higher proportion than the non-parental (recombinant) ones.

Let A and B be linked on one chromosome and a and b on its homologue (both parents AaBb with this arrangement).

1. **Complete linkage (no recombination):** each parent forms only the parental gametes AB and ab, in equal proportion.

| Gametes | AB | ab |
|---|---|---|
| **AB** | AABB (dominant for both) | AaBb (dominant for both) |
| **ab** | AaBb (dominant for both) | aabb (recessive for both) |

Phenotypes: dominant for both traits : recessive for both = **3:1**; no new combinations appear. (If each parent carried A with b and a with B, the result would be 1 Ab-type : 2 dominant for both : 1 aB-type.)

2. **Incomplete linkage:** a few recombinant gametes (Ab and aB) also form, so all four phenotypes appear, but the parental types far outnumber the recombinant types and the ratio deviates significantly from 9:3:3:1.
3. The proportion of recombinants depends on how closely the genes are linked: Morgan found only 1.3 per cent recombination between the tightly linked genes white and yellow, but 37.2 per cent between white and miniature wing in Drosophila.
groundedIn: §4.3.3; Fig. 4.11 — two linked genes did not segregate independently and the F2 deviated significantly from 9:3:3:1; parental combinations much higher than non-parental; recombination; tightly linked (1.3 per cent) and loosely linked (37.2 per cent) genes

stem: Briefly mention the contribution of T.H. Morgan in genetics.
solution:
**Thomas Hunt Morgan** and his colleagues provided the **experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance** and discovered the basis of linkage and recombination.

1. He worked with the fruit fly **Drosophila melanogaster**, which suits genetic studies: it grows on simple synthetic medium, completes its life cycle in about two weeks, a single mating produces a large number of progeny, the sexes are easily distinguished, and it has many hereditary variations visible under low power microscopes.
2. He carried out dihybrid crosses on **sex-linked genes** (e.g., yellow-bodied, white-eyed females \(\times\) brown-bodied, red-eyed males) and found that the \(\text{F}_2\) ratio deviated significantly from 9:3:3:1.
3. He coined the term **linkage** for the physical association of genes on a chromosome and **recombination** for the generation of non-parental gene combinations.
4. He showed that some genes are **tightly linked** (white and yellow, 1.3 per cent recombination) and others **loosely linked** (white and miniature wing, 37.2 per cent recombination).
5. His student **Alfred Sturtevant** used recombination frequency as a measure of distance between genes to map their positions on the chromosome, the basis of genetic maps.
groundedIn: §4.3.2; §4.3.3; Fig. 4.10; Fig. 4.11 — Morgan's experimental verification of the chromosomal theory with Drosophila and its advantages; sex-linked dihybrid crosses; coined linkage and recombination; 1.3 and 37.2 per cent recombination; Sturtevant's mapping

stem: What is pedigree analysis? Suggest how such an analysis, can be useful.
solution:
**Pedigree analysis** is the analysis of the inheritance of a particular trait over several generations of a family, represented as a family tree using standard symbols. Since controlled crosses cannot be performed in human beings, the study of family history is the alternative.

**Uses:**

1. It is a strong tool to **trace the inheritance** of a specific trait, abnormality or disease in a family.
2. It shows whether the trait is **dominant or recessive** (e.g., myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant, sickle-cell anaemia autosomal recessive).
3. It shows whether the trait is **autosomal or sex-linked**, as in haemophilia, an X-linked recessive trait passed from carrier females to male progeny.
4. It helps identify **carriers** of a disorder, e.g., Queen Victoria's pedigree shows many haemophilic descendants because she was a carrier.
5. It is used in **genetic counselling**, to predict the chance of a disorder appearing in the children of a couple.
groundedIn: §4.8.1; §4.8.2; Fig. 4.14 — pedigree analysis is analysis of traits over generations of a family since controlled crosses are not possible; traces a trait, abnormality or disease; dominant or recessive; sex-linked haemophilia; Queen Victoria a carrier; BEYOND CHAPTER: use in genetic counselling to predict the chance of a disorder in a couple's children

stem: How is sex determined in human beings?
solution:
Sex in human beings is determined by the **XY type** mechanism, and it is the **sperm** that decides the sex of the child.

1. Of the 23 pairs of chromosomes, **22 pairs are autosomes**, the same in both sexes; one pair is the **sex chromosomes**.
2. A female has **XX**; a male has **XY**.
3. The female produces only one type of ovum, carrying an X-chromosome (**homogametic**).
4. The male produces two types of sperm: **50 per cent with X** and **50 per cent with Y** besides the autosomes (**heterogametic**, male heterogamety).
5. Fertilisation:

| Ovum / Sperm | X | Y |
|---|---|---|
| **X** | XX (female) | XY (male) |

6. An ovum fertilised by an X-bearing sperm develops into a **female (XX)**; one fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm develops into a **male (XY)**.
7. Both kinds of sperm have an equal chance of fertilising the ovum, so in every pregnancy there is a **50 per cent** probability of a male or a female child.
groundedIn: §4.6; §4.6.1; Fig. 4.12 — XY type in humans; 22 pairs of autosomes; female XX produces one type of ovum, male produces 50 per cent X and 50 per cent Y sperm; male heterogamety; genetic makeup of the sperm determines sex; 50 per cent probability

stem: A child has blood group O. If the father has blood group A and mother blood group B, work out the genotypes of the parents and the possible genotypes of the other offsprings.
solution:
**Father: \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i; mother: \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i. Possible offspring genotypes: \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i, \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i and ii.**

1. ABO blood groups are controlled by gene I with three alleles, \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i; \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are completely dominant over i.
2. Blood group O has genotype **ii**, so the child received one i allele from each parent.
3. The father (group A) must therefore be **\(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i** and the mother (group B) **\(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i**.
4. Cross \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i \(\times\) \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i:

| Mother / Father | \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) | i |
|---|---|---|
| **\(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)** | \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) (AB) | \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i (B) |
| **i** | \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i (A) | ii (O) |

5. Other offspring may be \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) (group AB), \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\)i (group A) or \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\)i (group B), besides ii (group O), in the ratio **1:1:1:1**.
groundedIn: §4.2.2.2; Table 4.2 — gene I has three alleles IA, IB and i; IA and IB completely dominant over i; IA IB co-dominant giving AB; genotypes and blood types of offspring; ii is O

context: Explain the following terms with example
stem: Co-dominance
solution:
**Co-dominance** is the condition in which both alleles of a pair express themselves fully in the heterozygote, so the \(\text{F}_1\) **resembles both parents**.

**Example: ABO blood groups in human beings.**

1. The groups are controlled by gene I, with three alleles \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i, which decide the kind of sugar polymer on the plasma membrane of red blood cells.
2. \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) each produce a slightly different form of sugar; i produces none.
3. When \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are present together, **both express** their own types of sugar, so the red blood cells carry both A and B sugars and the person has blood group **AB**.
groundedIn: §4.2.2.2; Table 4.2 — in co-dominance the F1 resembles both parents; ABO blood groups controlled by gene I; IA and IB produce slightly different sugars, i none; IA and IB together both express, giving AB

context: Explain the following terms with example
stem: Incomplete dominance
solution:
**Incomplete dominance** is the condition in which neither allele is completely dominant, so the \(\text{F}_1\) has a phenotype **in between** the two parents.

**Example: flower colour in dog flower (snapdragon, Antirrhinum sp.).**

1. True-breeding red (RR) \(\times\) true-breeding white (rr) gives an \(\text{F}_1\) that is all **pink (Rr)**.
2. \(\text{F}_1\) self-pollinated (Rr \(\times\) Rr):

| Gametes | R | r |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | RR (red) | Rr (pink) |
| **r** | Rr (pink) | rr (white) |

3. \(\text{F}_2\): **1 red : 2 pink : 1 white**. The genotypic ratio (1:2:1) is as in any monohybrid cross, but the phenotypic ratio changes from 3:1 to 1:2:1, because R is not completely dominant over r and Rr can be told apart as pink.

Another example: in pea, Bb seeds produce starch grains of intermediate size between BB (large) and bb (small).
groundedIn: §4.2.2.1; Fig. 4.6; §4.2.2.2 — F1 in between the two parents; snapdragon RR x rr gives pink Rr; F2 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white; R not completely dominant over r; starch grain size in Bb pea seeds intermediate

stem: What is point mutation? Give one example.
solution:
A **point mutation** is a mutation that arises due to a change in a **single base pair** of DNA.

**Example: sickle-cell anaemia.** A single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene, **GAG to GUG**, replaces glutamic acid (Glu) by valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of haemoglobin. The mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen tension and changes the RBC from a biconcave disc to an elongated sickle-like shape.
groundedIn: §4.7; §4.8.2; Fig. 4.15 — mutation due to change in a single base pair of DNA is point mutation; sickle cell anemia is a classical example; GAG to GUG at the sixth codon; Glu replaced by Val; sickle shape under low oxygen tension

stem: Who had proposed the chromosomal theory of the inheritance?
solution: **Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri.** They noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes and used chromosome movement during meiosis to explain Mendel's laws. Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the **chromosomal theory of inheritance**. It was experimentally verified by Thomas Hunt Morgan and his colleagues.
groundedIn: §4.3.2 — Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted the parallel behaviour of chromosomes and genes; Sutton united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance; experimental verification by Morgan

stem: Mention any two autosomal genetic disorders with their symptoms.
groundedIn: §4.8.3; Fig. 4.16; §4.8.2; §4.5 — Down's syndrome trisomy 21 with short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, palm crease, retarded development; phenylketonuria autosomal recessive, phenylalanine not converted to tyrosine, phenylpyruvic acid, mental retardation, excreted in urine; reduction in hair and skin pigmentation
